view: The first prisoner, the cupbearer who dreamed of pressing grapes, will survive, leave prison, and resume serving wine to his master, the king.
note: Some notes give his return after three days; that timing is recorded separately.

words: وَأَمَّا ٱلْءَاخَرُ فَيُصْلَبُ فَتَأْكُلُ ٱلطَّيْرُ مِن رَّأْسِهِۦ
view: The other prisoner, the baker whose dream involved bread or baskets on his head, will be executed by crucifixion, and birds will eat from his head.
note: Some specify that the king executes him, that the birds eat after his death, or that this is punishment for his crime.

view: The cupbearer's three grape clusters or vine branches signify three more days in prison; on the fourth day he is released and restored to serving the king. One report describes a grape seed growing into clusters that he presses for the king; another reads the vine as the king and restored favor.
note: The reports differ in the vine imagery and whether they explicitly say release occurs on the fourth day.

view: The baker's three baskets signify three days before the king has him released and crucified, with birds eating from his head; one account places the crucifixion on the fourth day.
note: Accounts vary between execution after three days and on the fourth day.

view: Reports name the condemned baker Majlath, Majlatha, Malḥab, Mujlith, or Mujlab, and the restored cupbearer Nabu, Nabwa, or Bunū; the latter regains his master's favor and former post.
note: The transmitted names and spellings differ.

view: The two men share prison and a question, yet their fates diverge: one is saved and favored or elevated, while the other is killed.
note: The visions are read as foreshadowing rescue and destruction.

view: Rabbahu refers to the cupbearer's human master, the king; calling someone the lord of a house or estate is comparable usage.
note: Several notes explicitly identify this master as the king.

view: Joseph could infer that the prisoners served the king from their use of rabb for their master in the statements about serving wine and asking to be remembered.
note: The observation also concerns 12:42.

view: Saqā means handing someone a drink, whereas asqā ordinarily means providing a source of water or irrigation; most linguists preserve this distinction, despite a poem and some usage treating the verbs as synonymous.
note: Al-Naḥḥās prefers the distinction and cites Qur'anic usage against the poem; the other notes report both linguistic positions.

view: Saqā and asqā can both mean giving someone a drink; some linguists treat them as synonyms.
note: Other linguists distinguish giving a drink from providing water.

view: The common reading has active yasqī from saqā; another active reading uses yusqī from asqā, a verb also used for giving drink.
note: Al-Samīn compares a reading of 56:69.

view: ʿIkrima and al-Jaḥdarī are reported to read the verb passively, yusqā, with rabbahu nominative: the master or king is given wine to drink. One gloss says he is given drink until satisfied; another report adds riyyihi as a second object.
note: Al-Zamakhsharī attributes the passive only to ʿIkrima; Ibn Jinnī notes its parallel with the other prisoner's punishment.

view: ʿIkrima is reported to have recited the clause as أما أحدكما فيسقي ربه خمرا.
note: The note gives this wording without a further gloss.

view: Joseph repeats the address to his prison companions when he resumes their interpretation after teaching religion, signaling a new and important topic and drawing their attention to it.
note: The explanations emphasize either the change of subject or the importance of the answer.

view: Calling them prison companions evokes shared hardship, lowers worldly pretension, and softens their hearts toward friendship.

Joseph does not name which prisoner will be saved or condemned, sparing the condemned man and letting the men approach a painful conclusion gradually; each can hope for the favorable outcome until he asks for identification.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr's explanation depends on the verse preserving the order of Joseph's speech.

view: The verse may condense Joseph's actual speech, in which he directly assigned each interpretation to its prisoner.
note: This is an alternative to taking the verse's veiled summary as his exact speech.

view: The passive crucifixion verb reflects that only the king has authority to crucify.
The paired clauses use ellipsis: each stated fate implies the opposite outcome for the other man.
Qaḍā denotes fully completing or executing a matter; accordingly, the phrase says it is finished or settled, and the title qāḍī derives from this sense.
note: Al-Ṭabarī also speaks of God's decree taking effect.

view: Istiftāʾ means requesting a fatwa or clear answer to a difficult or uncertain matter; a fatwa supplies the answer itself rather than its underlying reason.
note: Al-Rummānī distinguishes an answer about meaning from one explaining cause.

view: The verb aftā retains its hamza; some link its root to fatā, youth, because a clear explanation strengthens its recipient.
The explanation of the word istiftāʾ was given earlier in the commentary on al-Nisāʾ.
The matter has been settled as a real, unavoidable outcome for the prisoners, whether their reported dreams were genuine or invented: one will be saved and the other killed.
note: This differs from the reading that only Joseph's answer or interpretation has been completed.

view: The statement means Joseph has completed the requested interpretation or answer; it need not guarantee that the predicted events will occur.
note: Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, and Qatāda are cited for this reading; it competes with revelation-based certainty.

view: The singular matter is the shared accusation or crime for which the prisoners were jailed, or its consequence: although their dreams differed, the case ends with one escaping and one dying.
note: Al-Ālūsī reports an implied word for the consequence of the accusation.

view: The singular matter refers to their shared question about what will happen to them during imprisonment, despite their distinct individual fates.
note: Al-Ālūsī prefers the eventual outcome and takes the preposition causally: they asked about dreams to learn their fate.

view: The settled matter is the dreams themselves as incidents being interpreted, rather than the men's eventual fates or the cause of their imprisonment; the prisoners' own singular wording accounts for one 'matter' despite two dreams.
note: An investigator argues from what an inquiry asks about and compares the king's request about his dream; al-Ālūsī rejects the distinction between dream and outcome as inconsistent.

view: Calling the dreams an 'affair' and the request an 'inquiry' magnifies obscure, momentous dreams; the present tense extends their request up to Joseph's completed answer.

Joseph's certain forecast came through revelation or God-given knowledge of the unseen, so his words announce a decree that will occur; the fulfillment of invented dreams is offered as evidence, and this certainty suits a prophet.
note: This competes with the view that interpretation was conjectural; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects conjecture because Joseph declares the matter settled and God taught him interpretation.

view: As a prophet, Joseph could be certain of what God caused him to say, unlike a nonprophet, even without a separate report of revelation.
note: This is offered as an alternative explanation of his certainty.

view: Joseph's statement may rest on dream interpretation or judgment without a guaranteed outcome; dream interpretation, even when true, proceeds by predominant probability.
note: Ibn ʿAbbās is cited for interpretation rather than revelation, with the later word ẓann offered as evidence; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects this account.

view: Joseph's interpretation became a binding decree because he was a prophet and God brought it about to confirm his prophethood; an ordinary false interpretation does not bind anyone.
Once a dream is interpreted, its outcome is fixed; this explains Joseph's declaration, and Ibn Kathīr extends it even to a dream someone invented.
note: Al-Qurṭubī distinguishes a prophet's interpretation from an ordinary false one.

view: A prophetic report says a dream remains suspended until interpreted, after which it occurs; another version likens it to resting on a bird's wing until told, when it falls.
note: The report transmitted by Abū Ruzayn also calls a dream one forty-sixth of prophecy and advises sharing it only with someone of judgment; Aḥmad's version is through Muʿāwiya ibn Ḥayda.

view: A prophetic report through Anas says a dream is realized according to its first interpreter.
note: Ibn Kathīr cites a version in Abū Yaʿlā's Musnad.

view: After Joseph gave the unfavorable interpretation, both prisoners said they had seen no dreams and had invented them to test him or had only been playing; Joseph said the decision stood.
note: Some reports only say they denied the dreams; others specifically say the dreams were fabricated.

view: In another account, only the prisoner condemned to crucifixion denies having dreamed after hearing the interpretation, saying they were playing or he had invented his dream.
note: This differs from reports that both men denied or fabricated their dreams.

view: Another account says the prisoners truly saw their dreams but denied them after disliking the interpretation; a cupbearer might have lied to protect his companion.
note: The reports differ on whether the dreams themselves were fabricated or only later denied.

view: A separate report says one of the two prisoners lied when describing a dream to Joseph.
note: It does not identify which prisoner lied.

view: One account has the prisoners accuse Joseph of lying after his interpretations; he responds that the matter is settled.
note: This differs from reports that the prisoners denied their own dreams.

view: Mujāhid says Joseph's interpretation had come true exactly when the young men claimed they had only been playing or had invented the dreams.
note: The last note attributes the claim that the interpretation had occurred to Ibn Masʿūd.

view: A report says Joseph delayed interpreting the dreams because one forecast execution; a royal meal had been sent to a prisoner marked for death, and he mentioned arriving food first to prompt their renewed request.
note: Attributed to Muḥammad ibn ʿAbbās in Ibn Abī Ḥātim's report through Ibn Jurayj.

view: A report of Ibn Jurayj merely quotes the phrase 'in which you seek a decision' without explaining it.

A report says a man told ʿUmar of a dream alternating lush growth and drought; ʿUmar predicted alternating faith and apostasy ending in death as an unbeliever, and the man then said he had dreamed nothing.
Such a prediction was exceptional for ʿUmar, whom the author describes as divinely inspired, with intuitions and statements that came true.
note: The source cites two further examples.

view: The prisoners' dreams may foreshadow the king's dream: pressed grapes correspond to green ears and fat cattle, while birds eating the baker's bread correspond to dry ears and lean cattle.
note: The link concerns 12:43.

view: The cupbearer's fate signifies the spirit's renewed attachment to pleasures after restraint from association.

The baker's crucifixion signifies suppressing desire and fixing it to vegetative nature so imagination and animal faculties cannot act through it; when desire dies, the soul's powers fulfill divine rights.
The declared outcome marks Joseph's approach to God and the rise of sainthood through annihilation in God.
The Qur'anic Joseph story illustrates God's unfathomable direction of human affairs: people may dislike what benefits them and love what harms them.
note: The source contrasts Genesis and cites 2:216.

view: Joseph uses the opportunity before interpreting the prisoners' dreams to invite them to monotheism, as prophets use opportunities to convey God's message.
Ibn ʿĀshūr reports that Egyptians of Joseph's time had about thirty gods representing natural forces or stars.
note: This supplies context for Joseph's preceding address to the prisoners.

view: A referenced form may be the plural of ʿashwa, 'darkness,' with its distinct portions motivating the plural.
note: The note does not identify a matching word in 12:41; its linguistic point is retained as supplied.
